planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Kent coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Selected in the 1920s from a single disease-tolerant tree found on the L.C. Kent estate near Mysore in southern India, this Typica-type Arabica became one of the first commercial cultivars bred specifically for partial resistance to coffee leaf rust. Its tall, upright growth and moderate yields resemble other heirloom Typica-derived lines, and it later served as one of the two parents behind the widely grown Indian hybrid S795. Give it the same dappled shade, warm humid air, and rich, well-drained acidic soil that other Arabica types need, and expect the same three-to-four-year wait before the first harvest. Because rust pressure has intensified since Kent's introduction, home growers in humid climates should still watch closely for orange leaf spotting even on this historically resistant line.
sources: World Coffee Research Arabica Coffee Varieties Catalog
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; S795 coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Released by Indian coffee researchers as a cross between the rust-tolerant Kent selection and the Ethiopian landrace Tafarikela, S795 combines good cup quality with sturdier disease tolerance than older heirloom Typica and Bourbon lines. It has become one of the most widely planted Arabica cultivars across South India, Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea for its dependable yields and adaptability to a range of elevations. Grow it like other Arabica coffees, with filtered shade, evenly moist, well-drained acidic soil, and protection from any temperature below 55F. Its moderate vigor and manageable size make it a reasonably forgiving choice for a large container or greenhouse planting.
sources: World Coffee Research Arabica Coffee Varieties Catalog
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; French Mission coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Brought from Ethiopia to the Congo basin and the Great Lakes region of East Africa in the early twentieth century by French Catholic missionaries, this Typica-type landrace became the genetic foundation for much of the Arabica coffee still grown today in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, and Burundi. It shares the tall, open, willowy growth habit typical of unimproved Typica-derived lines, along with a sweet, clean cup and only modest resistance to leaf rust and berry disease. Cultivate it with the same rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, dappled shade, and consistent warmth other heirloom Arabica types require, and allow extra headroom since it grows larger than compact modern hybrids. Because seed lots are less standardized than named commercial hybrids, expect some natural variability in vigor and cup character between individual plants.
sources: World Coffee Research Arabica Coffee Varieties Catalog
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Ocumare cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Named for the Ocumare valley along Venezuela's Aragua coast, this fine-flavor Criollo-type landrace has been propagated there as a series of numbered clonal selections prized by chocolate makers for bright, fruity, low-bitterness flavor notes distinct from the more floral Porcelana strain grown further west. Like other true Criollo cacaos it is thin-shelled, slow to establish, and notably more vulnerable to fungal pod disease than robust Forastero-type trees, so it rewards attentive humidity and airflow management. Plant seedlings in spring beneath the canopy of taller shade trees in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil, and keep air temperatures reliably above 60F year-round. Expect a long wait of four to five years before the tree produces a meaningful first harvest of pods.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
